title: R-Ch-M
hookLine: rachamim, mercy, shares a root with rechem, womb

lines: HER BOWELS YEARNED UPON HER SON.
cards: Two women stand before King Solomon with one baby between them. They share a house; each had a son; one child died in the night, and now each says the living one is hers. No witnesses.
No proof. The king calls for a sword and gives an order that makes the whole court go still: divide the living child in two, and give half to each. One woman breaks.
The King James says it in old, physical words: "for her bowels yearned upon her son." The other says, let it be neither mine nor yours. What moves inside the first woman is today's root.

teach.b: R-Ch-M. Resh, chet, mem. Turn it four ways.
First, the body. Voice these letters one way and you have rechem, the womb. Voice them another way and you have rachamim, mercy, compassion.
The same letters hold the place a child grows and the feeling that protects it. Second, back to the courtroom. What the King James calls bowels is, in Hebrew, her rachamim, stirring.
And look at what that mercy does. She gives up her own claim: give her the living child, she says, and in no wise slay it. She would rather lose him to the other woman than to the sword.
Solomon hears it and knows at once who the mother is.

teach.h: HER BOWELS YEARNED: MERCY AS EVIDENCE.
teach.b: Mercy is the evidence. Third, not only mothers.

teach.h: AS A FATHER PITIETH HIS CHILDREN.
teach.b: A psalm uses the root for a father: "Like as a father pitieth his children, so the LORD pitieth them that fear him." Pitieth is racham.
The womb-love picture stretches to anyone who loves the way a parent loves, and then again, to God. Fourth, a name for God.
Jewish prayer calls God ha-Rachaman, the Merciful One; in the grace after meals, a run of short requests each opens with that word.
Sitting at a table, full, people address God by a name built from a womb. So mercy here isn't a cool decision handed down from a bench.
It's the feeling that rises from the gut when someone small is in danger, and acts before thinking.

how: Jewish prayer calls God ha-Rachaman, the Merciful One, and in the grace after meals a series of requests each begins with that name; rachamim, mercy, is asked for throughout the daily prayers.

o: fairness, giving each side exactly half
pity felt from a distance, without acting
mercy, from the same letters as the womb

p: her bowels yearned upon her son

s: in Hebrew, womb and mercy are built from the same three letters
rechem and rachamim: resh, chet, mem.
the psalm keeps this mercy for mothers only
"like as a father pitieth his children": the same root.
Solomon gave the baby to the woman who argued hardest for it
he gave it to the one who would give it up to save its life.

games.q: you're King Solomon. two women both claim the same baby. there are no witnesses. what do you do?
o: give the child to whoever spoke first.
call for a sword and order the child divided.
send them both away to settle it.
games.why: the sword. the real mother's rachamim break out, she gives up her claim to save him, and that mercy shows the king who she is.

practice: Bring to mind someone who's let you down lately, not badly, just enough to sting, and picture them small, five years old in a kitchen doorway, trying and failing.
Let the feeling shift if it wants to, and ask what a loving parent would say to that child: not excuses, just mercy. If you pray, you can ask the Merciful One for mercy for them, and for yourself.

wordCard.voice: R-Ch-M. Resh, chet, mem: rechem, the womb, and rachamim, mercy, the love that protects what it carries. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: mercy, compassion. the same letters as rechem, womb.

carryVoice: Your line: mercy is womb-love. It protects what it carries. See you tomorrow.
